name: Water cutting / dehydration

lead: Water cutting is the deliberate reduction of body water, through fluid restriction, sweating, sweatsuits and saunas, to look drier, leaner and more defined. It is borrowed from combat sports, where athletes cut to a lower weight class before weigh-ins, and is also referred to in bodybuilding for a dry look.

Because sweat is mostly water, weight lost this way is largely fluid, so the leaner look shows within hours and comes back with rehydration. The method is well documented in weigh-in sports, where sports medicine commentary describes it as dangerous.

paras: Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading beforehand, exercise-induced sweating, sweatsuits and saunas, usually timed within days or hours of a weigh-in or photo. The effect is temporary and reverses once fluids are replaced.

Dehydration can cause headache, fatigue, confusion, seizures, heatstroke, hypernatremia and kidney problems. Losses of 15 to 25 percent of body water are described as fatal, and several weight-cutting athletes died in 2015, 2016 and 2017. Some organizations have changed their rules in response.

angle.text: Shedding body water through fluid restriction, sweating and saunas gives a visibly leaner, sharper look within hours, a method borrowed from combat-sports weight cuts. The result is temporary and the method carries documented dehydration risks, including deaths in weight-cutting athletes.

lead: Water cutting, also called a dehydration cut, water manipulation or, in combat sports, the water cut, is the practice of deliberately reducing body water for a short period to look leaner or weigh less. Physique competitors use it in the final stage before a show to sharpen muscle definition and vascularity, combat-sport athletes use it to reach a lower weight class, and some people in looksmaxxing and fitness circles use sweating, fluid restriction or sauna sessions to look drier, with a tighter face and clearer jawline.[1][2]

Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading beforehand, and sweating through exercise, sweat suits or saunas.[1] Bodybuilding descriptions note that competitors combine carbohydrate loading and dehydration in the final stage for maximum definition and vascularity.[2] The idea is that water held under the skin softens the outline of muscle and facial structure, so reducing it makes edges and veins look sharper for a short period.

Research on the practice comes mostly from sports science. A 2018 questionnaire of 81 British natural bodybuilders found carbohydrate, water and sodium manipulation to be the most common peaking strategies, and a 2021 critical review concluded that evidence supporting peak-week protocols is scarce.[3] In combat sports, a 2019 systematic review of 16 studies reported average rapid weight loss of about 10 percent of body mass in MMA cohorts.[3] Several deaths of athletes who were cutting weight between 2015 and 2017 led organisations to change their rules.[1]

paras: Weight cutting is described as having two forms: losing fat and muscle over weeks before an event, and losing water in the final days.[1] Some athletes diet and add aerobic exercise instead, aiming to improve their strength-to-mass ratio.[1] The practice is used in combat sports, rowing and equestrian sports, where a lower weight is an advantage.[1]

In physique sports the final stage is called peak week. Bodybuilding sources describe pairing carbohydrate loading with dehydration for definition and vascularity, and competitors typically also tan and shave before going on stage.[2] In the 2018 survey of British natural bodybuilders, only 6.2 percent kept their regular diet the week before competing, and many used water loading or restriction to reduce water retention.[3] Interviews with seven experienced natural bodybuilders likewise described fluid and sodium manipulation with carbohydrate loading in peak week to improve leanness and vascularity.[3]

Combat-sport athletes follow a similar pattern before weigh-ins, then regain much of the weight before competing. A questionnaire of 637 competitors across seven combat sports found MMA athletes reported the highest sauna use (76 percent) and water loading (67 percent), and that skipping meals was more common in taekwondo and wrestling.[3] A 2012 review put the prevalence of rapid weight loss across combat disciplines at about 50 percent.[3]

The look sought is a drier, tighter appearance: visible muscle separation, vascularity and, in the face, more defined cheekbones and jaw. Reports from practitioners vary. One T Nation member posted before-and-after pictures from a water cut with a difference of about 15 lb in water weight and described very little visible change.[4]

Reviewers of natural bodybuilding preparation describe dehydration and electrolyte manipulation in the final hours and days as potentially dangerous and possibly not improving appearance, while a 2021 review lists the aims of peak-week practice as maximising muscle glycogen and reducing subcutaneous water and bloating.[3] Dehydration itself is described as producing sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes among its signs.[5]

A comprehensive review of dehydration physiology distinguishes between loss of water from inside cells and iso-osmotic loss from the extracellular space, and discusses assessment by osmolality and volume.[6] A consensus statement from a multidisciplinary group defines dehydration and reviews diagnostic methods and clinical implications.[7]

Dehydration signs include thirst, headache, nausea, reduced urine, confusion and in severe cases seizures. Acute complications include hypovolemic shock, coma, heatstroke and hypernatremia, and rehydrating too quickly risks cerebral oedema.[5]

By total body water lost, Wikipedia describes 1 to 2 percent as mild and able to impair cognitive performance, 5 to 8 percent as producing fatigue and dizziness, over 10 percent as causing physical and mental deterioration, and 15 to 25 percent as fatal. Rehydrating too rapidly risks cerebral oedema, and dehydration can cause hypernatraemia.[5]

Variants include gradual dehydration over several days, same-day sauna or sweatsuit sessions, water-loading followed by restriction, and sodium and carbohydrate manipulation in peak week.[1][3] The methods reviewers list for combat sports also include laxatives, diuretics and plastic or rubber suits, which a 2012 review describes as harmful to performance and health.[3]

Related practices include extended fat-loss cutting phases, which bodybuilding sources date from about 12 to 14 weeks before competition, and training-camp weight monitoring by organisations.[2][1] Reviews of physique athletes recommend weight loss of no more than about 0.5 to 1 percent of body mass per week in preparation and note higher rates of disordered eating and body-image concerns.[3]

Reported deaths while cutting weight include Yang Jian Bing, a 21-year-old Chinese fighter, in December 2015, Scottish Muay Thai fighter Jordan Coe in March 2016, and Australian Jessica Lindsay in November 2017.[1] ONE Championship banned dehydration-based cutting later in December 2015, replaced pre-fight weigh-ins with 'walking weight' measurements and added urine specific gravity hydration testing up to three hours before bouts.[1]

Physician Paddy Golden told the Western Australia Combat Sports Commission in December 2017 that acute water loss is very dangerous and, in June 2018, that deaths were inevitable without regulation, urging hydration tests for bout eligibility.[1] In February 2022 the Mohegan Tribe Department of Athletic Regulation suspended a fighter for six months and fined him $2,500 after he posted a video of himself vomiting during a weight cut before Bellator 274.[1]

Bodybuilding's Wikipedia article links contest preparation, including extreme weight changes and intentional dehydration, with higher mortality and sudden cardiac death among bodybuilders, alongside performance-enhancing drug use.[2] A 2023 review of premature death in bodybuilders notes that research is limited and confounded, and calls for more study.[3]

No controlled studies were found of deliberate water cutting for physique or facial appearance. Sports-science work covers adjacent ground. A 2019 systematic review of 16 studies (4,432 combat athletes) reported rapid weight loss of about 7.4 kg (roughly 10 percent) and regain of a similar amount in two MMA cohorts, with athletes able to compete up to three weight categories above their weigh-in class.[3] A 2020 systematic review of 14 judo studies (1,103 athletes) found physiological results conflicting, psychological results more consistent (more tension, anger and fatigue, less vigour), and performance evidence ambiguous.[3] A 2019 narrative review said cuts of about 5 percent of body mass in under 24 hours impair repeat-effort performance.[3]

For physique sport, a 2021 critical review, a 2014 narrative review and a 2018 survey describe water, sodium and carbohydrate manipulation as common but weakly evidenced, with authors raising possible health harms and doubtful effect on appearance.[3] A 2016 study of 27 women dieting for fitness competition for four months reported about 12 percent body weight loss and hormonal changes that mostly recovered within 3 to 4 months of increased intake.[3]

Research on dehydration more broadly includes a 2018 meta-analysis of 33 studies finding that dehydration impairs cognitive performance,[8] a review of cognition and mild dehydration describing impaired attention and memory at about 2 percent loss,[9] and randomised trials of mild dehydration and mood in young men and women.[10][11]

Public coverage has focused on combat-sport deaths and on regulators' responses, such as ONE Championship's hydration testing and the 2022 Bellator suspension.[1] Nutrition experts, as summarised by Wikipedia, rarely advise on cutting weight safely and generally recommend against it, although many athletes do it for a competitive edge.[1] Researchers studying Swedish elite combat athletes describe weight regulation as also serving mental functions of focus and commitment.[3]

lore.intro: Water cutting comes up in bodybuilding and strength forums as part of peak-week routines and as a way to appear leaner on camera. Accounts vary widely in how much visual change they report.[4]
